name: Mok
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.verdict: a source was named but could not be reached
earlier_scan.source_named: Tannumsaeng, Phakawee. 2020. A Preliminary Grammar of Mok, Hwe Koi Variety, Chiang Rai (MA thesis, Payap University; Glottolog grammar sketch)

sources.citation: Tannumsaeng, Phakawee. 2020. A Preliminary Grammar of Mok, Hwe Koi Variety, Chiang Rai, with Special Focus on the Anaphoric Uses of tɤ́ʔ. MA thesis, Payap University, Chiang Mai. xi+157 pp. (Glottolog 589716; downloaded from Internet Archive copy of ic.payap.ac.th/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/)
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: Nothing. Sec. 1.7 'Phonology' (pp. 7-8), summarising Hall & Devereux (2018), gives 19 consonants, 9 monophthongs + 3 diphthongs, reduced syllables m̩ n̩ ɲ̩ ŋ̩ pə tə kə sə, 'two distinctive tones' (low, high), vowel length not contrastive (p. 13); the words stress/accent/prominence/iambic do not occur anywhere in the thesis.

sources.citation: Hall, Elizabeth. 2017. On the linguistic affiliation of 'Tai Loi'. Journal of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society 10.2: xix-xxii. hdl:10524/52409
sources.note: Nothing; a 4-page note on the exonym 'Tai Loi' covering Angkuic (Muak Sa-aak) and Waic groups; no Mok phonology.

sources.citation: Hsiu, Andrew. 2015. The Angkuic languages: a preliminary survey. Handout, ICAAL 6, Siem Reap (Zenodo 1127808).
sources.note: Nothing on stress; p.1 'All Angkuic languages are tonal (cf. Svantesson 1988, 1991)'; sec. 3 'Mok' (p. 5) only lists three kinds of Mok (Lampang, Shan State, Muak Sa-aak) with no phonological data.

sources.citation: Sidwell, Paul. 2021. Northern Austroasiatic languages of MSEA. In Paul Sidwell & Mathias Jenny (eds.), The Languages and Linguistics of Mainland Southeast Asia, 499-546. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton.

sources.access_detail: a digital copy exists, behind a library sign-in (also a publisher record (DOI), probably paywalled)
sources.note: Most recent handbook treatment of Palaungic/Angkuic typology; may give a family-level statement on iambic/sesquisyllabic word stress applicable to Mok (second-hand at best).

sources.citation: Shintani, Tadahiko. 2019. The Sen Tsum (I-Mok) language. Linguistic Survey of Tay Cultural Area (LSTCA) no. 121. Fuchu, Tokyo: Research Institute for Languages and Cultures of Asia and Africa (ILCAA). ISBN 978-4-86337-300-6.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: print only (no digital copy found when the work was looked up)
sources.note: Independent first-hand documentation of a Shan State Mok (I-Mok/Sen Tsum) variety; Shintani's LSTCA volumes open with a phonological outline (syllable structure, tones) that may comment on stress of presyllables.

sources.citation: Hall, Elizabeth & Shane Devereux. 2018. Preliminary Mok phonology and implications for Angkuic sound change. Paper presented at the 28th Annual Meeting of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society (SEALS 28), Wenzao Ursuline University, Kaohsiung, 17-19 May 2018.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: The only dedicated phonological description of Mok proper (five Shan State varieties); the source behind Tannumsaeng's inventory; most likely place for a statement on word/presyllable stress and tone-stress interaction.

sources.citation: Owen, R. Wyn. 2018. Initial findings from Mok KIQ and DMT. Unpublished manuscript, SIL International (Mainland Southeast Asia).
